---
title: "Coming from NetworkX"
description: >
  A map from NetworkX to knappnet for Python users meeting the R package
  first, with the conventions that differ and how to reproduce NetworkX's
  numbers.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

knappnet's engine is written in Rust and reached through a small C
interface, so every language runs the same code. The R package comes
first; **a Python package is planned** and will share the engine, the
conventions, and the validation suite described here. Until then, this
guide is for Python users working in R, and a preview of what the Python
package will look like.

[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) is one of the reference tools every knappnet measure is checked
against (see [validation](validation.html)), and `convention = "networkx"`
reproduces its choices where they differ from the default, which follows
[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/).

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## The data model

In [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) a graph is a dictionary of dictionaries, and attributes live on
nodes and edges as key-value pairs. In knappnet a network is two data
frames, which is what `nx.from_pandas_edgelist()` and
`nx.to_pandas_edgelist()` already move between:

```python
import networkx as nx
import pandas as pd

edges = pd.DataFrame({"source": ["ana", "ana", "ben", "cy", "cy"],
                      "target": ["ben", "cy", "cy", "dee", "eli"]})
G = nx.from_pandas_edgelist(edges)
nx.betweenness_centrality(G, normalized=False)
```

```{r}
edges <- data.frame(source = c("ana", "ana", "ben", "cy", "cy"),
                    target   = c("ben", "cy", "cy", "dee", "eli"))
g <- net_frame(edges, directed = FALSE)
net_betweenness(g)
```

Results are vectors in the order of `g$nodes`, not dictionaries keyed by
node. `setNames(net_betweenness(g), g$nodes$name)` gives the keyed form, and
`g$nodes$betweenness <- net_betweenness(g)` stores the result as a column.

Two more differences matter:

- **Direction is a property of the network,** set with `directed =`
  (default `TRUE`), as with `nx.DiGraph` versus `nx.Graph`. Parallel edges
  are always allowed, as in `nx.MultiGraph`; nothing needs to be declared.
- **Weights are used by default.** Most NetworkX functions ignore weights
  unless you pass `weight="weight"` (or `distance=`). A knappnet network
  with a weight column uses it in every measure that can, and
  `weighted = FALSE` ignores it. Weights are distances unless the network
  is created with `weight_type = "strength"`.

## Function map

| [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) | knappnet | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `nx.Graph()`, `nx.DiGraph()`, `nx.MultiGraph()` | `net_frame(edges, nodes, directed)` | |
| `nx.from_pandas_edgelist(df)` | `net_frame(df)` | Endpoints are the first two columns unless `from`, `to` name others. |
| `G.add_nodes_from(...)` with attributes | the `nodes` data frame | Isolates need a row in `nodes`. |
| `nx.to_numpy_array(G)`, `nx.to_scipy_sparse_array(G)` | `as.matrix(g)`, `as.matrix(g, sparse = TRUE)` | |
| `nx.from_numpy_array(A)` | `net_from(A)` | |
| `nx.read_graphml()`, `read_gexf()`, `read_gml()`, `read_pajek()`, `node_link_graph()` | `net_read(file)` | Format from the extension. |
| `nx.write_graphml()`, ... | `net_write(g, file)` | |
| `G.degree()` | `net_degree(g)` | |
| `G.degree(weight="weight")` | `net_strength(g)` | |
| `nx.degree_centrality(G)` | `net_degree(g) / (nrow(g$nodes) - 1)` | |
| `nx.betweenness_centrality(G)` | `net_betweenness(g, normalized = TRUE, convention = "networkx")` | NetworkX normalizes by default; knappnet does not. The convention matters only with parallel edges. |
| `nx.closeness_centrality(G)` | `net_closeness(g, convention = "networkx")` | Wasserman-Faust scaling for disconnected networks; distances *to* the node in directed networks. |
| `nx.harmonic_centrality(G)` | `net_harmonic(g, convention = "networkx")` | Not normalized; distances to the node. |
| `nx.eigenvector_centrality_numpy(G)` | `net_eigen(g, convention = "networkx")` | Unit Euclidean norm; NetworkX refuses disconnected networks, and so does this convention. |
| `nx.density(G)` | `net_density(g, convention = "networkx")` | Differs from the default only for a single node. |
| `nx.connected_components(G)` | `net_components(g)$membership` | A membership vector instead of a list of sets. |
| `nx.weakly_connected_components()`, `strongly_connected_components()` | `net_components(g, mode = "weak" / "strong")` | |
| `nx.core_number(G)` | `net_coreness(g)` | NetworkX rejects loops and multigraphs; knappnet counts them as [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) does. |
| `nx.find_cliques(G)` | `net_max_cliques(g)` | |
| `max(len(c) for c in nx.find_cliques(G))` | `net_clique_number(g)` | |
| `nx.community.louvain_communities(G, seed=)` | `net_louvain(g, seed = )` | A membership vector with a `modularity` attribute. Partitions differ between implementations; modularity is comparable. |
| `nx.community.modularity(G, communities)` | `net_modularity(g, membership)` | NetworkX returns 0 for a network without edges; knappnet returns `NaN`. |
| `nx.constraint(G)`, `nx.effective_size(G)` | `net_constraint(g)`, `net_effective_size(g)` | NetworkX counts self-loops as ties to oneself; knappnet ignores them, as Burt's measures concern ties to others. |
| (none) | `net_efficiency(g)` | Burt's efficiency, effective size over the number of contacts (not `nx.local_efficiency()`). |
| `nx.triadic_census(G)` | `net_triad_census(g)` | NetworkX accepts only directed graphs. |
| (none) | `net_brokerage()`, `net_struct_equiv()`, `net_concor()` | |
| (none) | `net_qap_cor()`, `net_mrqap()` | QAP correlation and MRQAP regression. |
| (none) | `net_centralization()`, `net_fragmentation()` | |

PageRank, Katz centrality, assortativity, ego networks, bipartite
(two-mode) networks, and layouts are coming soon.

## Reproducing NetworkX's numbers

**Closeness on disconnected networks.** [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) scales closeness by the
share of the network a node reaches (Wasserman and Faust 1994, p. 201), so
a node in a small component is not mistaken for a central one:

```{r}
split <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "b", "d"), target = c("b", "c", "e")),
                  directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node     = split$nodes$name,
           networkx = round(net_closeness(split, convention = "networkx"), 3),
           igraph   = round(net_closeness(split, normalized = TRUE), 3))
```

**Parallel edges in betweenness.** NetworkX walks neighbor sets, so two
parallel edges are one route; [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and knappnet's default count each
edge as a distinct shortest path. In this network `a` and `b` are joined
twice:

```{r}
multi <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "b", "a", "d"),
                             target   = c("b", "b", "c", "d", "c")), directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node     = multi$nodes$name,
           igraph   = round(net_betweenness(multi), 3),
           networkx = round(net_betweenness(multi, convention = "networkx"), 3))
```

Between `a` and `c` there are three shortest paths under the default (two
through `b`, one per parallel edge, and one through `d`), and two under
NetworkX's.

**Eigenvector scale.** NetworkX scales scores to unit length, igraph so
that the largest is 1. The ranking is the same:

```{r}
kite <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4),
                            target   = c(2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 4, 5)), directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node     = kite$nodes$name,
           igraph   = round(net_eigen(kite), 3),
           networkx = round(net_eigen(kite, convention = "networkx"), 3))
```

**Weighted shortest paths with ties.** Reciprocals of whole-number weights
can give paths whose lengths are equal in exact arithmetic but differ in
the last bit of floating point (1/3 + 1/6 versus 1/2). NetworkX compares
lengths exactly and keeps only one of the tied paths; knappnet, like
igraph, treats lengths within a relative 10<sup>-10</sup> as equal, and
agrees with an exact-arithmetic evaluation of the definition. On such
networks NetworkX's weighted betweenness can differ; the validation
suite records the cases.
